issues.body: axis_exceeds compares against total + total * BUDGET_REL_TOL, so for every positive total it deliberately accepts a representable spent + charge that is greater than total but within the relative 1e-12 allowance. This is smaller than the prior absolute slack and fixes delta_total = 0, but it still contradicts the documented rule that a charge exceeding either total is refused fail-closed and the claimed basic-composition bound. The added small-delta test charges exactly 1e-13 and then attempts a whole second 1e-13; it does not exercise a just-over-budget value inside the relative allowance.
issues.fix_hint: Do not add a positive acceptance tolerance to the configured delta total. Implement a conservative comparison/accounting representation that cannot authorize cumulative delta above the configured total (for example exact/fixed-point accounting with validated conversion, or a deliberately upward-rounded charge/downward-rounded remainder). Add a regression test whose cumulative delta is representably just above a positive total by less than total * 1e-12 and assert refusal without mutation. If epsilon rounding accommodation is retained, document and justify it separately rather than applying the same overspend rule to cryptographic failure probability.
issues.title: Relative tolerance still authorizes spend above the configured privacy budget

verdict.summary: Round 5 is stagnant: the fixed absolute 1e-12 allowance was replaced by a relative allowance, which correctly closes the zero-delta hole and greatly reduces the magnitude of possible overspend, but it does not satisfy the prior round's requested fail-closed invariant. axis_exceeds still authorizes spent + charge values strictly above the configured total whenever the excess is at most total * 1e-12. The new tests cover a zero total and an exact tiny-total boundary, but no just-over-boundary charge within the new relative slack. Because the public documentation claims basic sequential composition and fail-closed refusal above either total, knowingly authorizing any positive excess remains a major correctness issue.
